statements.text: AI governance is the set of policies, regulations, standards and institutional frameworks that guide how AI is developed, deployed and overseen, at organizational, national and international levels.
statements.explanation: The glossary's definition spans all three levels. A company's internal review process, a national framework such as NIST's, and a regional law such as the EU AI Act are all governance. The common thread is structure that decides who may do what with an AI system and who answers for it.

statements.text: AI governance refers only to national laws; an organization's internal policies and review processes are not part of it.
statements.explanation: The glossary's governance framework entry is explicitly about the policies, processes, roles and tools inside an organization or jurisdiction. Most governance that touches a given system is internal: who approves a deployment, what gets logged, when a human must review. Law is one layer, not the whole.

statements.text: Accountability in AI means that identifiable people or organizations are answerable for a system's outcomes, including mechanisms for redress when it causes harm.
statements.explanation: The glossary ties accountability to two things: a named party and a path to remedy. A policy that assigns no one, or that offers no way for an affected person to seek correction, fails the standard even if it is otherwise detailed. Naming the responsible party is the first governance act.

statements.text: The accountability gap is the delay between an AI incident and the publication of its postmortem.
statements.explanation: The accountability gap is the situation where no single party can be held responsible for harm, because decisions are spread across developers, deployers and users in a complex supply chain. It is about diffusion of responsibility, not timing. Closing it means assigning answerability before anything goes wrong.

statements.text: When an AI system causes harm, responsibility automatically rests with the model's original developer alone.
statements.explanation: The glossary's accountability gap entry exists because responsibility is distributed: a developer trains the model, a deployer configures and ships it, a user operates it. Which party answers depends on contracts, regulation and the decision in question. Assuming it is always the developer is one way the gap opens.

statements.text: An AI audit is a systematic evaluation of a system against regulations, ethical guidelines and performance standards, and may include technical testing, documentation review and stakeholder consultation.
statements.explanation: The glossary's definition is broader than a test run. Technical checks establish what the system does; documentation review establishes whether that matches what was claimed; stakeholder consultation establishes whether affected people experience it as intended. A full audit draws on all three.

statements.text: An AI audit is purely a technical accuracy test, so documentation and stakeholder views fall outside its scope.
statements.explanation: Documentation review and stakeholder consultation are named components in the glossary's definition. An accurate model deployed against its documented limits, or one that is technically sound but harmful to a group nobody consulted, would pass a pure accuracy test and fail an audit.

statements.text: An audit trail for an AI system records only the final deployed model version, since earlier decisions are irrelevant once it ships.
statements.explanation: The glossary defines the audit trail as a chronological record of all decisions, actions and changes throughout the lifecycle. Incident investigation depends on the history: which data was chosen, which evaluation was skipped, who approved the change. A snapshot of the final version answers none of that.

statements.text: An impact assessment evaluates an AI system's potential effects on individuals, communities and society before and during deployment, and some regulations require one.
statements.explanation: The glossary pairs the general impact assessment with the algorithmic impact assessment that some jurisdictions mandate for automated decision systems in high-stakes uses. The timing matters: the point is to find foreseeable harms while there is still a choice about whether and how to deploy.

statements.text: An impact assessment is carried out once, after deployment, to record what the system turned out to do.
statements.explanation: The glossary says before and during deployment. An assessment written only afterward is an incident report, not an assessment. The regulatory versions exist to put a documented evaluation in front of the deployment decision, with ongoing review as the system and its context change.

statements.text: Algorithmic transparency is the degree to which an algorithm's logic, rules and data dependencies are visible and understandable to affected people, regulators and the public.
statements.explanation: The glossary's definition names the three audiences. Transparency to a regulator may mean access to documentation and testing; transparency to an affected person may mean a plain-language explanation of a decision. Both are part of the same principle applied at different depths.

statements.text: The transparency paradox is the tension between opening an AI system up for accountability and the risks that disclosure brings, such as enabling attacks or exposing proprietary information.
statements.explanation: The glossary names the trade-off directly. Publishing a system's full logic helps auditors and also helps adversaries craft inputs against it. Governance work lives in that tension, choosing what to disclose to whom, rather than treating more disclosure as free.

statements.text: Full transparency carries no downside, so publishing every detail of an AI system is always the right governance choice.
statements.explanation: The transparency paradox exists because disclosure has costs: adversarial attacks become easier and proprietary or sensitive information can leak. Responsible disclosure norms, where a vulnerability goes to the developer before the public, are one answer. Transparency is a value to be weighed, not an absolute.

statements.text: Training data transparency means disclosing the sources, composition, collection methods and known biases of the data a system was trained on, and it is a growing regulatory requirement.
statements.explanation: The glossary frames it as both a responsible-AI practice and an emerging legal demand. Datasheets for datasets, which document motivation, composition, collection and intended use, are the standardized form. Without it, downstream users cannot judge what a model's behavior reflects.

statements.text: The right to explanation holds that a person subject to an automated decision is entitled to a meaningful account of the logic involved, and it is partially codified in the GDPR's Article 22.
statements.explanation: The glossary's entry cites the article directly and its GDPR provisions entry adds the right not to be subject to purely automated decisions and the requirement for data protection impact assessments. For deployers, the practical consequence is that a decision must be explainable to the person it affects.

statements.text: The GDPR says nothing about automated decision-making; it only regulates how personal data is stored.
statements.explanation: The glossary's GDPR provisions entry lists the right not to be subject to purely automated decisions, data protection impact assessments and transparency requirements. The right to explanation traces to Article 22. Any deployment that makes decisions about EU residents has to account for it.

statements.text: Human-in-the-loop design has a person review, approve or modify AI outputs before they are acted upon.
statements.explanation: The glossary defines it that way and names the uses: high-stakes decisions, quality control and maintaining accountability. Praxis's own policy applies it, with every AI-assisted change reviewed by a person before publication. The loop is the place where responsibility is exercised.

statements.text: Human-in-the-loop means a person monitors a dashboard and is informed of the system's decisions after they have taken effect.
statements.explanation: The glossary's definition puts the human before the action: review, approve or modify before the output is acted upon. A person informed afterward can investigate but cannot prevent, which is monitoring rather than oversight. The distinction matters most in exactly the high-stakes cases the pattern is for.

statements.text: Provenance tracking applies only to media files; models and training data have no provenance worth recording.
statements.explanation: The glossary defines provenance tracking as recording and verifying the origin and history of data, models and AI system components across the lifecycle, and names accountability, reproducibility and supply chain security as the reasons. Media provenance, such as C2PA, is one application among several.

statements.text: The C2PA coalition develops technical standards for certifying the source and history of media content through cryptographic provenance metadata.
statements.explanation: The glossary names the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity and its approach: metadata signed so that edits and origins can be verified rather than asserted. It is a complement to watermarking, which hides a pattern in the content itself, and to detection, which analyzes artifacts.

statements.text: An AI watermark is a visible logo placed in the corner of a generated image.
statements.explanation: The glossary defines an AI watermark as hidden patterns in generated content that allow its synthetic origin to be detected, proposed for text, images and audio alike. Detection algorithms look for the statistical pattern embedded during generation. A visible badge is a label, not a watermark.

statements.text: Watermarking is a solved, universal system: every AI generator embeds one and every platform can detect it.
statements.explanation: The glossary describes watermarking as proposed for identifying AI content, and detection as algorithms that look for patterns embedded by specific systems. Coverage depends on which generators participate and which platforms check. It is one tool against misinformation, not a guarantee of attribution.

statements.text: Synthetic media refers only to video deepfakes; AI-generated text does not count.
statements.explanation: The glossary's definition covers images, video, audio and text generated or substantially modified by AI, and names deepfakes, AI art, voice cloning and large language model outputs together. Disclosure rules written around synthetic media reach generated text as well.

statements.text: Deepfake regulation ranges from disclosure requirements to criminal penalties for malicious deepfakes.
statements.explanation: The glossary describes laws targeting the creation and distribution of synthetic media along that spectrum. The lighter end requires labeling; the heavier end criminalizes specific harms such as non-consensual intimate imagery or election deception. Jurisdictions differ on where they draw the lines.

statements.text: AI disclosure requirements are obligations to tell people when they are interacting with an AI system rather than a human, and they appear in the EU AI Act and in US state laws.
statements.explanation: The glossary's entry names both sources. The Responsible AI policy records how Praxis meets them: an ethics ticker on every page, commit attribution and a dedicated transparency page. For a chatbot deployer the minimum is making the AI nature of the interaction clear up front.

statements.text: Disclosure only matters for AI-generated images; a chatbot has no obligation to reveal that it is an AI.
statements.explanation: The glossary's disclosure entry is about interacting with an AI system rather than a human, which is the chatbot case precisely. Image labeling falls under synthetic media and deepfake rules. Both are disclosure, aimed at different moments where a person might otherwise be misled.

statements.text: An AI transparency report is a public document disclosing an organization's AI systems, their capabilities, limitations, known biases and safety measures.
statements.explanation: The glossary models it on corporate social responsibility reporting. Praxis's Responsible AI policy is a small example: it inventories every AI system used, states what each does with data, and publishes a risk self-assessment with residual risk levels. The point is that outsiders can check the claims.

statements.text: AI incident databases are kept private by developers, since publishing failures would help no one.
statements.explanation: The glossary describes the AI Incident Database as a public repository maintained by organizations such as the Partnership on AI, so that others can learn from failures. Incident reporting is modeled on aviation and healthcare, where shared records of accidents and near-misses drive systemic improvement.

statements.text: Reporting AI incidents is pointless, because every failure is unique and teaches nothing transferable.
statements.explanation: The glossary's incident reporting entry says the opposite: shared reports enable pattern recognition and systemic improvement. Bias drift, hallucination in a particular workflow and prompt injection through a document are recurring classes. Aviation's safety record rests on exactly this kind of reporting.

statements.text: Responsible disclosure for AI means privately reporting a discovered vulnerability or dangerous capability to the developer before making it public, allowing time for mitigation.
statements.explanation: The glossary's definition balances two goods: the developer gets time to fix the issue, and the public eventually learns of it. Praxis's security policy invites exactly this, asking reporters to describe the issue and steps to reproduce, and offering credit with permission once resolved.

statements.text: A datasheet for a dataset lists file sizes and formats and nothing about how the data was collected or what it is meant for.
statements.explanation: The glossary's entry on datasheets for datasets lists motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, intended uses, distribution and maintenance. The collection and intended-use sections are the governance payload: they tell a downstream team whether the data fits their purpose and whose consent it rests on.

statements.text: AI literacy is the knowledge and skill needed to understand, evaluate and interact with AI systems, and is treated as essential for informed consent and democratic participation.
statements.explanation: The glossary's entry names informed consent, democratic participation and workforce adaptation. Disclosure only works when the person told they are talking to an AI knows what that implies, which is why literacy sits beside transparency in governance frameworks rather than being a separate concern.

statements.text: Praxis Library's governance is self-governed with community oversight, with its governance documents, audit tooling and source code public on GitHub, and a formal third-party audit on the roadmap.
statements.explanation: The Responsible AI policy's independent verification section describes the current status in exactly those terms. The interim mechanisms are public code, a documented audit methodology, a human verification loop with screenshot proof and a full commit history. External certification is planned as the project scales.

statements.text: Praxis Library has completed a formal independent audit certification such as SOC 2 or ISO 27001.
statements.explanation: The policy lists formal third-party audit under Roadmap with the status Planned. It records an independent governance assessment that rated the framework highly, but that is an assessment, not a certification. Open-source transparency and community review are named as the interim verification.

statements.text: Under the EU AI Act, Praxis Library classifies itself as minimal risk: an educational website with no personal data processing and no high-risk AI deployment.
statements.explanation: The policy's compliance matrix records the classification and the reasoning, and notes that its voluntary transparency measures exceed what that tier requires. The general-purpose model provisions are marked not applicable because the site uses AI tools without providing or deploying models.

statements.text: The public audit report separates errors, which must be fixed, from warnings, which flag best-practice gaps, and info items, which are inventory notes rather than problems.
statements.explanation: The audit report page defines the three levels. Errors are confirmed violations of enforced standards such as an inline script breaking the content security policy. Warnings do not fail the audit but each carries a fix suggestion. Info records counts and statuses so nothing is silently skipped.

statements.text: The counts on Praxis Library's audit report are typed in by hand and updated when someone remembers.
statements.explanation: The page states that the site snapshot is auto-discovered from the live filesystem with no hardcoded counts, and that all values are dynamically discovered by the audit script. The report is the script's output rendered, which is what makes it a transparency artifact rather than a claim.

statements.text: Praxis Library's acceptable use policy allows teaching, sharing and citing its content with attribution, and asks users not to misrepresent authorship or use the content to circumvent safety measures in AI systems.
statements.explanation: The policy's permissions are learn, teach, share and cite, with a link back to the source page. Its three requests are to keep attribution, not to present the content as original work, and not to use it to create misleading AI content, manipulate others or bypass safety measures.

statements.text: Praxis Library's site policy presents its content as professional advice suitable for high-stakes decisions.
statements.explanation: The site policy states the opposite: the content is educational, not professional advice, and is meant for learning and practice rather than replacing expert guidance for high-stakes decisions. It adds that the verify-before-relying principle applies to the site's own content too.

statements.text: Praxis Library's risk self-assessment names dependence on a single AI provider as a risk and mitigates it by being a static site with no runtime AI dependency.
statements.explanation: The policy's AI provider dependency entry rates the likelihood low and the residual risk minimal. The reasoning is architectural: all AI output is committed as plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the site would run indefinitely without any provider, and the methodology is documented so human developers could continue alone.
